question: How do we know the universe is expanding?

research.claim: We know the universe is expanding because the dark lines in distant galaxies' light are shifted toward red, more for farther galaxies, and the shift grows in proportion to distance (Hubble's law, about 70 km/s for every megaparsec, 3.26 million light years). Light from a receding source arrives with longer waves; and a pattern in which speed grows in proportion to distance is what every galaxy sees when all the distances between galaxies grow by the same share, so no galaxy is the centre. Running the growth back gives a hot, dense beginning about 13.8 billion years ago.
research.explanation: With every distance scaled by a factor a(t), the separation of galaxies i and j is a(t) x_ij, so their relative speed is (da/dt / a) times their separation: H0 times distance, the same from every galaxy. Light emitted when the scale was a_then arrives with its wavelength multiplied by a_now/a_then (the cosmological redshift); for nearby galaxies the shift z is about v/c. 1/H0 for H0 = 70 km/s/Mpc is 977.8/70 = 14.0 billion years; with gravity's slowing and dark energy's later speeding up, the measured age is about 13.8 billion years.
assumptions: A growth rate of 70 km/s per megaparsec; measurements range from about 67 to 73.

Hydrogen's lines at 410, 434, 486 and 656 nanometres, which hot hydrogen (as in stars' outer layers) absorbs and glowing hydrogen emits; cold hydrogen does not absorb at these colours. Chapter 1 slides them by 8%.
The row stands for galaxies far apart; nearby galaxies and anything bound by gravity or other forces do not spread apart.
The plot's scatter is made up for the picture.
The glow's waves in chapter 6 stretch from orange to microwaves; the true stretch since the glow set off is about 1,100 times.
research.prediction: A galaxy twice as far as another shows about twice the redshift, and the same proportion holds whichever direction we look.
research.falsifier: If distant galaxies' lines showed no shift, or shifts that did not grow with distance, or galaxies in some directions approached as often as others receded, this explanation would be wrong.
limitations: Very distant galaxies need the full theory (general relativity), in which redshift is not simply proportional to distance.
The picture leaves out the expansion's slowing and later speeding up.
Hubble's own 1929 value was about 500 km/s per megaparsec, too high because of errors in his distances; today's measurements give about 67 to 73.
misconceptions: The galaxies are flying away from a centre where an explosion happened.
Everything, including atoms and the solar system, is expanding.
Nothing can move away from us faster than light.

Can galaxies move away faster than light?

sources.title: Hubble's law (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: Galaxies move away from Earth at speeds proportional to their distance; attributed to Edwin Hubble's 1929 work, using Cepheid variable stars to find distances; the Hubble constant is around 70 km/s/Mpc (Planck 67.4, other measurements near 70 and 73); the raisin-bread analogy; type Ia supernovae as standard candles.

sources.title: Expansion of the universe (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: To any observer, all but the nearest galaxies (bound by gravity) move away at speeds proportional to their distance; the ant-on-a-balloon analogy; recession of distant objects is not limited by the speed of light, which applies to local reference frames; picturing galaxies as stationary while space stretches is often argued erroneously.

sources.title: Redshift (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: The cosmological redshift is commonly attributed to the stretching of photons' wavelengths as the universe expands.

sources.title: Spectral line (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: Spectral lines identify atoms and molecules, like fingerprints.

sources.title: Age of the universe (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: The age of the universe is estimated at about 13.77 to 13.79 billion years.

sources.title: Cosmic microwave background (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: Light released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, when the universe was about 3,000 K, now arrives as a black-body glow at 2.72548 K, brightest in microwaves; discovered by accident in 1964 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson with a radio antenna, Nobel Prize 1978.

scene.title: How do we know the universe is expanding?
scene.subtitle: Almost every distant galaxy's light arrives redder than it should, and the farther the galaxy, the redder. What does that tell us?
scene.why: The light from far galaxies carries a clue, discovered a century ago: almost all of them are moving away from us, and from each other.
scene.opening: How do we know the universe is expanding?
scene.takeaway: Distant galaxies' hydrogen gaps have slid toward red, more the farther away they are. Their light arrives stretched because the gaps between galaxies keep growing; farther ones have more growing gaps between, so they move away faster. Every galaxy sees that same pattern, so there is no centre. Run it backwards, and everything was packed hot and dense 13.8 billion years ago; that glow, stretched ever since, still arrives as faint microwaves.

questions.a: No. Atoms, people, the Earth, the solar system and our own galaxy are held together by forces and gravity, and nearby galaxies are bound to each other too. Only the gaps between galaxies far apart grow.

There isn't one. Every galaxy sees the others moving away in the same pattern, faster the farther they are, as the row of galaxies in chapter 4 shows. As far as we can tell, the universe has no edge to measure a middle from.

questions.q: How do we know how far the galaxies are?
questions.a: By stars of known true brightness. Hubble used Cepheid stars, which pulse at a rate that tells how bright they really are; how faint they look then gives the distance. Today exploding stars called type Ia supernovae reach much farther.

questions.q: Can galaxies move away faster than light?
questions.a: Very distant ones, yes: their distance from us grows faster than light could cross it. That doesn't break the speed limit, which applies to things moving past each other nearby, not to the growth of distances across the universe.

If each galaxy had always kept its speed, its distance divided by its speed gives the time since all were together: about 14 billion years, the same for every galaxy. Gravity's slowing and dark energy's later speeding up nearly cancel, and the full calculation with today's best measurements gives 13.8 billion.

questions.q: Has anyone picked up that glow?
questions.a: Yes, by accident at first. In 1964 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson found a faint hiss in their radio antenna that came from every direction, day and night: it was this glow. It earned them the 1978 Nobel Prize.
The distance light travels in a year: about 9.5 trillion kilometres. A galaxy a million light years away is so far that its light set off a million years ago.

beats.title: Redder than it should be
beats.body: Pass a star's light through a prism, and it fans out into a rainbow. Hydrogen in the star always takes out the same four colours, like markers. In a distant galaxy's light, those four gaps have all slid toward red.

beats.title: Stretched light
beats.body: Each colour of light is a wave with its own spacing from crest to crest. As a galaxy moves away, each crest sets off farther from us, so they spread out. Longer waves look redder, and the stretch tells us how fast it goes.

beats.title: Farther means faster
beats.body: In 1929 Edwin Hubble plotted galaxies' speeds against their distances. A galaxy twice as far off is moving away about twice as fast. Today we find about 21 km a second more for each million light years away.

beats.title: No centre
beats.body: In this row, every gap between neighbouring galaxies grows by the same amount. Two gaps away, two gaps grow at once, so that galaxy pulls away twice as fast. Stand on any other galaxy and you see the same pattern, so none is the centre.

beats.title: Stretched on the way
beats.body: So 'moving away' really means the space between galaxies keeps growing. Light crossing those growing gaps is stretched along with them. The farther it travels, the more it stretches and reddens.

beats.title: Running it backwards
beats.body: Run this growth backwards, and the galaxies crowd ever closer. Long ago, all of space was packed so hot and dense it glowed: the Big Bang. Its glow, stretched past red ever since, arrives as unseen microwaves.

provenance.intro_note: This investigation was made in a coding session, not by the daily run: an AI coding agent built the picture and wrote the guide from sources retrieved in that session, on the owner’s pick, and AI reviewers checked it with the render checks, an accuracy review, a visual review, a first-time-reader test with a subtitle edit, and a blind-viewer test. It passed them in three rounds (the first found a wrong opening fact about hydrogen and pictures that suggested a centre), and their copy edits were then applied. Later the same day, at the owner’s request (the rainbow with dark lines and the grid of arrows were hard to follow, and the ending could be cooler), it was revised in a coding session: chapter 1 now shows a star’s light passing through a prism, with hydrogen’s four gaps as markers that a distant galaxy’s light shows slid toward red; chapters 4 and 5 use one row of galaxies, with matching arrows from two of them; and the ending runs back to a hot glow everywhere, then shows that glow’s waves, stretched into microwaves, reaching a radio dish today. The revision passed the render checks and all four reviews in two rounds, and their edits were applied.
